steps.say: Writers organise texts into paragraphs. Each paragraph is about one main idea.
Start a new paragraph for a new time, place, topic or speaker.
steps.show: new time, new place, new topic, new speaker

steps.say: Reports use subheadings, so readers can find information quickly.
steps.show: What they look like / Hunting and eating / Young dragons

steps.say: Letters, diaries, news reports and playscripts each have their own layout.
steps.show: News report: headline, who, what, when, where, quotes

steps.say: Writers choose words on purpose. Similes and strong verbs help us picture things.
steps.show: The notes bounced around the hall like rain on a tin roof.

check.prompt: When should a writer start a new paragraph?

options.why: A paragraph usually has several sentences about one idea.

options.text: when the topic or the time changes

options.why: Paragraphs are needed all through a text.

options.text: whenever they use a long word
options.why: Long words have nothing to do with paragraphs.

hints: A paragraph is about one main idea.
What happens when the writer moves on to something new?
Think about the sections of the Komodo report.
check.explanation: A new paragraph starts when the writer moves to a new topic, time, place or speaker.

check.prompt: What does the first paragraph of a news report usually tell you?

options.why: That would not belong in a news report.
News reports start with the key facts.

hints: News readers want the key facts quickly.
Think about the first paragraph of the school garden report.
What did it tell you straight away?
check.explanation: The first paragraph of a news report gives the key facts: who, what, when and where.
